p: Then he wrote his father's name, and died.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The Louisiana Tigers on Cemetery Hill”, paragraph 6 of 9

p: On the summit, Carroll's Union brigade counterattacked. Without Confederate infantry support coming behind them, Hays and the survivors of Avery's command could not hold. They came back down the hill in the darkness, back through the town, back to their starting line.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The Louisiana Tigers on Cemetery Hill”, paragraph 7 of 9

p: They had touched the crest. They had held the guns. They had come closer to breaking the Union center than any Confederate force at Gettysburg.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The Louisiana Tigers on Cemetery Hill”, paragraph 8 of 9

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The Louisiana Tigers on Cemetery Hill”, paragraph 9 of 9

p: Colonel Edward Porter Alexander was twenty-eight years old, the chief of artillery for Longstreet's corps, and the man responsible for directing the greatest artillery bombardment in the history of the Western Hemisphere.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Alexander's Two Messages”, paragraph 1 of 14

p: For two hours, 170 Confederate guns had been firing at Cemetery Ridge. The Union guns had fallen mostly silent. To Alexander, watching from Seminary Ridge through the smoke and dust, it looked like the cannonade might have worked. The ridge appeared quieter.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Alexander's Two Messages”, paragraph 2 of 14

p: But Alexander was running out of ammunition. The Confederate army had no ammunition reserve close enough to replenish the batteries before the infantry assault. When the guns stopped firing, there would be nothing left for close support.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Alexander's Two Messages”, paragraph 3 of 14

p: He wrote his first message to Pickett:

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Alexander's Two Messages”, paragraph 4 of 14

p: 'General: If you are to advance at all, you must come at once or I cannot give you proper support, but the enemy's fire has not slackened materially and at least eighteen guns are still firing from the Cemetery itself.'

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Alexander's Two Messages”, paragraph 5 of 14

p: Pickett showed the message to Longstreet. Longstreet, who had spent two days arguing against this assault, could not speak. He bowed his head.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Alexander's Two Messages”, paragraph 6 of 14

p: Alexander watched the ridge. The Union guns were still silent. He wrote a second message:

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Alexander's Two Messages”, paragraph 7 of 14

p: 'For God's sake come quick. The eighteen guns have gone. Come quick or my ammunition won't let me support you properly.'

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Alexander's Two Messages”, paragraph 8 of 14

p: Pickett came to Longstreet. 'General, shall I advance?'

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Alexander's Two Messages”, paragraph 9 of 14

p: Longstreet turned away. He could not order it. He bowed his head again.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Alexander's Two Messages”, paragraph 10 of 14

p: Pickett understood. He rode to his division.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Alexander's Two Messages”, paragraph 11 of 14

p: Alexander never forgot what he had done. In his memoir, written decades later, he wrote that when he sent that first message he had not understood what he was setting in motion — that he was, in effect, writing the death warrant for thousands of men. If he had known the ammunition supply was nearly gone, he wrote, he would have urged Longstreet to stop the assault entirely.
